main.title: UC Berkeley CS 61C: Great Ideas in Computer Architecture
main.why: C and number representation, RISC-V assembly, the datapath and five-stage pipeline, caches, SIMD and thread-level parallelism, and virtual memory. In English.

main.title: A New Golden Age for Computer Architecture
main.why: How instruction sets went from microcode to RISC, why general-purpose speedups stalled, and why domain-specific chips and open ISAs come next.

main.title: The Case for the Reduced Instruction Set Computer
main.why: Compilers used little of ever larger instruction sets, whose complexity slowed single-chip designs, so RISC keeps a few simple instructions.

main.title: An Efficient Algorithm for Exploiting Multiple Arithmetic Units
main.why: Execution units idled behind instructions waiting on results, so Tomasulo's algorithm renames registers with tags and starts each instruction when its operands arrive.

main.title: A case for (partially) TAgged GEometric history length branch prediction
main.why: Each wrong branch guess flushes a deep pipeline, so TAGE matches branch histories of increasing length against tagged tables and uses the longest match.

main.title: Spectre Attacks: Exploiting Speculative Execution
main.why: CPUs run ahead on predicted branches and discard wrong work, but Spectre shows that work leaves cache traces that leak another program's secrets.

further.title: Mitigating Spectre and Other Security Threats: The Cloudflare Workers Security Model

main.title: Flipping Bits in Memory Without Accessing Them: An Experimental Study of DRAM Disturbance Errors
main.why: As DRAM cells shrink they disturb their neighbors, and this RowHammer study shows repeatedly opening one row flips bits in nearby rows on most modules.

further.title: Introducing Half-Double: New hammering technique for DRAM Rowhammer bug

main.why: Hardware counters traced Jira's slowdown on Graviton to L3 misses and TLB walks, so Atlassian shrank the JIT code cache and enabled huge pages.

further.title: Adopting Arm at Scale: Transitioning to a Multi-Architecture Environment

main.title: A Low-Overhead Coherence Solution for Multiprocessors with Private Cache Memories
main.why: Broadcasting every cache write saturated the shared bus, so the protocol later named MESI marks blocks exclusive or shared and invalidates only for shared ones.

main.title: Shared Memory Consistency Models: A Tutorial
main.why: Write buffers, caches and compilers reorder memory accesses, so this tutorial explains the relaxed consistency models and the fences that restore order.

further.title: x86-TSO: A Rigorous and Usable Programmer's Model for x86 Multiprocessors

main.why: Container launches made every core fight over the kernel's mount lock, worst on dual-socket, hyperthreaded and mesh-interconnect CPUs, so Netflix cut the mounts per layer.

further.title: Seeing through hardware counters: a journey to threefold performance increase

main.title: Scalable Parallel Programming with CUDA
main.why: GPUs had become many-core processors, so CUDA exposes them through thread blocks, shared memory and barriers that scale across any number of cores.

main.title: Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures
main.why: Peak compute says little when memory bandwidth limits a kernel, so the Roofline model bounds performance by the operations done per byte moved.

main.title: In-Datacenter Performance Analysis of a Tensor Processing Unit
main.why: Neural network inference was outgrowing Google's datacenters, so the TPU drops caches and speculation for a large matrix unit and software-managed memory.

further.title: TPU v4: An Optically Reconfigurable Supercomputer for Machine Learning with Hardware Support for Embeddings
Inside the hardware and co-design of MTIA

main.title: Profiling a warehouse-scale computer
main.why: Benchmarks did not look like datacenter code, so Google profiled its live fleet and found instruction-fetch stalls and many cycles in shared low-level libraries.

main.title: Cores that don't count
main.why: Some cores in a large fleet silently compute wrong results that factory tests missed, so Google argues software must detect and isolate them.
